title: Active listening
summary: The learnable skill of listening to understand another person's full meaning - the content and the feeling behind it - and showing that understanding back to them, while holding off judgment, advice and persuasion until they confirm you have understood.
selfCheck: Could I state their point, and how they feel about it, well enough that they would say "yes, exactly"?
Did I hold back advice, reassurance and my own counter-argument until they confirmed I understood?
Was my attention on them, or was I rehearsing my reply or glancing at a screen?
Did I ask at least one question that drew out something they had not yet said?
Would they leave this conversation feeling heard, even if I did not agree with them?

title: Active voice
summary: Writing sentences so the person or organisation doing the action is the grammatical subject ("The team will send the report"), rather than the thing acted on ("The report will be sent"), so readers can see who does what.
selfCheck: Can the reader tell, sentence by sentence, who is responsible for each action?
Where I kept a passive, is the actor unknown, unimportant or obvious, or am I hiding who decided?
Did I mislabel any sentence as passive just because it uses "was" or describes the past?
steps: Find each sentence that has a form of "to be" plus a past participle (was sent, will be reviewed, has been approved).
Ask who does the action; if the sentence does not say, decide who should, and name them.
Rewrite with that actor as the subject and a strong verb right after it ("Finance will review the budget").
Address the reader as "you" when they are the one who must act.
Keep a passive only when the actor is unknown, unimportant or obvious, or when the thing acted on is what the paragraph is about.

example.situation: A project manager tells a client team what happens before go-live.
example.before: The test results will be reviewed and any outstanding issues must be resolved before the release can be approved.
example.after: Our QA lead will review the test results by Tuesday. Your team needs to fix any open issues by Thursday, and then I will approve the release.
example.why: The original names no one, so each side can assume the other owns the work; the rewrite assigns every action to a person and a date.

title: Anxiety reappraisal
summary: Reinterpreting the racing heart and jitters before a talk, interview or other evaluated performance as useful energy or excitement - rather than trying to calm down - so that the arousal is treated as a resource for the task instead of a sign of threat.
selfCheck: Am I trying to force myself to feel calm, or accepting that being keyed up is normal before something that matters?
What is one thing that could go well in this talk, and have I pointed my energy at it?
Am I using the reframe as a substitute for preparing and rehearsing out loud?
After the talk, am I judging it by what the audience did, or by how nervous I felt?
steps: Expect your heart rate, breathing and alertness to rise before the talk, and stop treating that as proof that something is wrong.
Remind yourself, in a sentence, what the arousal is for - it moves oxygen and attention to where you need them for the task.
Just before you start, say "I am excited" (aloud or under your breath) instead of telling yourself to calm down.
Turn the excitement toward the opportunity - name one thing that could go well, such as the decision you want the audience to make.
Pair the reframe with preparation and rehearsal; it changes how the nerves feel, not whether you know your material.
Afterwards, judge the talk by what the audience understood or decided, not by how anxious you felt.

example.situation: A finance analyst is about to present a quarterly variance review to the leadership team for the first time and notices her hands shaking in the corridor.
example.before: Calm down, calm down. They'll see I'm nervous. Just get through the slides without messing up.
example.after: My heart's racing because this matters - that's energy I can use. I'm excited to show them why the logistics overspend is a one-off and get the forecast approved.
example.why: The first version fights the arousal, which rarely works, and keeps attention on what could go wrong. The second accepts the arousal, labels it as excitement and points it at a concrete opportunity - the shift the reappraisal studies tested.

title: Aristotle's Rhetoric
summary: Aristotle's fourth-century BCE treatise defining rhetoric as the ability to see the available means of persuasion in a given case; it introduced the three proofs of character, emotion and argument, and the first systematic analysis of how an audience shapes a speech.

title: Audience analysis
summary: The practice of working out, before you write or speak, who will receive a message, what they already know, what they care about and what they need to do with it, and then shaping the content, structure, tone and channel to fit them.
selfCheck: Who will read or hear this - including people copied or forwarded to - and which of them is the one who must act?
What does my primary audience already know, and which of my terms or steps would they not recognise?
What is in this for them, and do they see it in the first few lines?
Have I checked my picture of the audience against something they actually said or did, or am I only guessing?
steps: List every audience, not just the addressee - the decision maker, technical reviewers, people who are copied, people the message may be forwarded to and people affected by the outcome.
For the primary audience, write down what they already know, what they care about, what attitude they are likely to bring and what they must decide or do after reading.
Check your assumptions against evidence - the questions people actually ask you, past replies, usage data or a short conversation with a typical reader.
Choose content, order, vocabulary, tone and channel to fit the primary audience, putting what matters to them first.
Give secondary audiences their own clearly labelled section instead of mixing material for different readers.
Reread the draft as each audience in turn - including someone it might be forwarded to - and fix what would confuse or alienate them.

example.situation: An engineering lead emails a delay notice about a data-platform migration to a list that includes the client's finance director.
example.before: Heads up - the ETL refactor slipped because the CDC connector kept OOMing on the backfill. New ETA is sprint 14, assuming infra gets us the bigger nodes.
example.after: Subject: Data migration finishing three weeks later than planned (no change to cost). The move to the new reporting system will finish on 4 December instead of 13 November. Your month-end reports will run on the old system as usual until then. Technical details for your IT team are in the section below.
example.why: The finance director is the primary reader and needs the date, the impact on her work and the cost; the jargon and team shorthand move to a separate section for the technical secondary audience.

title: BATNA
aliases: best alternative to a negotiated agreement
summary: Working out, before you negotiate, the best thing you will actually do if this negotiation fails - and using that alternative as the yardstick for every offer, the basis of your walk-away point and a source of leverage you can deliberately improve.
selfCheck: Do I know concretely what I will do tomorrow if this negotiation ends without a deal?
Have I compared my alternative with the offer on equivalent terms, or only on the headline price?
Is my opening ask set by my goal, or have I let a weak alternative drag it down?
Is everything I am about to say about my alternatives true?
steps: Before the first meeting, list every realistic thing you could do if no deal is reached - other vendors, other candidates, building it in-house, waiting, or doing nothing.
Translate each alternative into the same terms as the deal on the table (total cost, scope, risk, timing, effort to switch) so you are comparing like with like.
Pick the single best alternative - that is your BATNA - and from it set your reservation value, the worst deal you would still accept over walking away.
Spend some preparation time improving the BATNA itself (get a real competing quote, line up a second option) rather than only describing it.
Estimate the other side's BATNA too, and ask about their alternatives, so you know how much they need this deal.
Anchor your opening ask on your goal, not on your BATNA; keep a weak BATNA to yourself and never invent an alternative you do not have.
Re-check the BATNA whenever new information arrives during the talks, and walk away only when an offer is genuinely worse than it.

example.situation: An operations manager is renegotiating an annual software contract after the vendor proposes a 12% price rise.
example.before: We really can't move away from you, so please do what you can on the price. What's the best you can offer?
example.after: We've priced a comparable tool that would cost us about 8% less in year one, including migration. We'd rather stay - the team knows your product - so we're looking for a renewal at last year's rate with the new reporting module included. What would make that work on your side?
example.why: The manager did the BATNA homework first (a real, like-for-like competing quote), so the ask is anchored on a goal rather than on desperation, the alternative is mentioned truthfully without a threat, and the question invites the vendor to solve the problem with them.

title: Bottom line up front
summary: Opening a message with its conclusion, recommendation or request - the one thing the reader must know or do - and only then giving the background and supporting detail.
selfCheck: If my reader read only the subject line and first two sentences, would they know what I need from them and by when?
Have I stated my conclusion or recommendation, or only described the situation and left the reader to infer it?
Is this message an exception - serious bad news, or a reader who expects context first - and have I chosen the structure on purpose?
steps: Before drafting, write one sentence that states your conclusion, recommendation or request, including any decision and deadline you need.
Make that sentence (after a short purpose statement if the format calls for one) the opening of the message, and echo it in the subject line or title.
Add only the background the reader needs to act on it, most important first, and move history and method to the end or an attachment.
Put any secondary requests or audiences in clearly labelled sections below the main point.
Reread only the first two lines and ask whether a busy reader could act on them alone; if not, rewrite them.
Decide deliberately whether this message is an exception - serious bad news or a reader who expects context first - and if so use an indirect structure on purpose rather than by habit.

example.situation: A project analyst emails her director about a vendor problem that needs a decision.
example.before: Hi Sam, I wanted to give you some background on the reporting vendor. Over the last two months we have seen several late deliveries, and after a call with their account team on Tuesday it looks like their new platform will not support our quarterly export. I have looked at a few options...
example.after: Subject: Decision needed by Thursday - switch reporting vendor for Q1. Sam, I recommend we move the Q1 reports to our backup vendor; it adds about two weeks of setup but keeps the March board deadline. Please approve or decline by Thursday. Background: our current vendor's new platform cannot produce the quarterly export (confirmed on Tuesday's call), and deliveries have been late twice since September.
example.why: The recommendation, the decision asked for and the deadline appear in the subject line and first two sentences, so the director can act without reading the history, which is still there for anyone who wants it.

title: Camera-optional norm
summary: An explicit team agreement that webcams are a choice rather than a requirement in video meetings, set per meeting type and modelled by the person running the meeting, so people can rest from being on camera without being judged for it.
selfCheck: Have I said out loud, or written in the invite, whether cameras are expected in this meeting and why?
Would a new team member feel safe turning their camera off here, and have I told them so?
Am I modelling the norm, or does my own always-on camera quietly signal that video is required?
When cameras are off, do I still give everyone a clear way to contribute?
steps: List your recurring video meetings and decide for each whether faces add value - small working sessions, sensitive one-to-ones and first meetings with new people usually benefit; large updates, webinars and long all-hands rarely do.
Agree the camera expectation for each meeting type with the team, write it in the invite or team charter, and say plainly that cameras-off is fine wherever video is not needed.
Tell newer colleagues directly, in person or one-to-one, that turning the camera off will not count against them.
Model it as the organiser - switch your own camera off for part of a long meeting or for audio-only segments, because people follow what they see others doing.
Keep participation visible without video - ask people by name, use chat, reactions or a shared document, and agree that cameras-off still means no multitasking.
When video is used, suggest hiding self-view once framing is set, and build in short audio-only breaks in meetings longer than about 45 minutes.

example.situation: A team lead runs a daily 30-minute stand-up and two weekly hour-long planning calls for eight people, several of whom joined in the last three months.
example.before: Invite text - 'Cameras on please, it helps us stay connected.' The lead keeps a full gallery view, comments when a tile is dark, and the newest analysts never switch off even on their fourth call of the day.
example.after: Team charter line - 'Stand-up: cameras optional. Planning: cameras on for the first 10 minutes of check-in, optional after. 1:1s: your call.' The lead turns their own camera off after the check-in, calls on people by name, and tells new joiners in their first 1:1 that cameras-off is normal here.
example.why: The expectation is explicit and tied to the purpose of each meeting, the lead's behaviour shows the norm is real, and the people under the most self-presentation pressure hear it said to them directly, while the check-in keeps the group connection that buffers fatigue.

title: Channel selection
summary: Deliberately choosing the medium for a message - in person, video, phone, chat, email or a document - according to whether the job is to transmit information or to build shared understanding, how much tone and feedback matter, and what the receiver needs to do with it.
selfCheck: Am I mainly passing information on, or do we need to reach agreement - and does my channel fit that job?
If my reader misread the tone of this text, what is the worst plausible interpretation, and would a call prevent it?
Am I choosing email or chat because it suits the message, or because it lets me avoid an awkward conversation?
After a live discussion, have I put the decision, owners and dates in writing?
steps: Name the job of the message in one line - is it mainly to pass on information the receiver can absorb alone (conveyance), or to agree on meaning, resolve disagreement or decide something together (convergence)?
For conveyance - updates, data, instructions, reference material - default to a written, asynchronous channel the receiver can reread and process in their own time.

For convergence - an ambiguous problem, a disagreement, a sensitive or emotional message, or a request you need someone to say yes to - default to a live channel with voice and fast feedback, such as a call, video or a face-to-face conversation.

If tone, sarcasm or humour carries part of the meaning, either move to voice or rewrite the text so the meaning survives without your tone of voice; read it aloud in a deliberately flat or opposite tone before sending.
Combine channels when the task needs both - send the facts in writing first, discuss live, then confirm the decision and owners in writing.
Check the receiver's side - their familiarity with you and the topic, time zone, norms and access - and adjust the default; a lean channel works better between people who already share context.

example.situation: A project manager needs a client's sign-off to cut a feature so the release can stay on date, and the client sponsor is known to be attached to that feature.
example.before: Email, sent at 6 pm - Subject: Scope change. Hi Priya, given the integration issues we will need to drop the reporting module from the March release. Let me know if that works. Thanks.
example.after: Short email first - Subject: Decision needed Thursday - reporting module vs. March date. Priya, I'd like 20 minutes Wednesday to talk through a trade-off: keep the March date by moving the reporting module to April, or keep the module and slip to mid-April. One-page options summary attached. Then a 20-minute call to discuss, followed the same day by a written recap of the decision, owner and new dates.
example.why: The facts travel in writing where they can be reread, the contested decision happens live where questions and concerns surface immediately, and the written recap locks in the shared understanding the call produced.

title: Communicating uncertainty to decision makers
aliases: conveying what is and is not known
summary: The skill of telling the people who must decide what you know, how precisely you know it, how solid the evidence is and what you are doing to learn more - stated as specifically as your knowledge allows rather than hidden, hedged into vagueness or inflated into false certainty.
selfCheck: Have I given a number or range where I have one, instead of a word like "probably" or "should be fine"?
Have I said separately how good the evidence behind my estimate is?
Have I told them what we do not yet know, what we are doing to find out and when we will know?
Am I presenting real disagreement among experts or data as such, rather than smoothing it over or overplaying it?
Is the uncertainty in the sentence that carries the estimate, not in a footnote or a later slide?

example.situation: A product lead tells the leadership team how many customers a pricing change will cost.
example.before: Churn should be fine - we don't expect much impact, though obviously nobody can be sure.
example.after: Our best estimate is that 3% of accounts cancel in the first quarter, with a plausible range of 1-6%. The estimate rests on a four-week pilot in one region, so confidence is moderate. We will know much more after the second region's renewals on 15 March; until then I'd budget for 6%.
example.why: The before version mixes false reassurance with a blanket hedge, so leaders can neither plan nor challenge it; the after version gives a point estimate, a range, the quality of the evidence and when it will improve, which is what a decision needs.

title: Curse of knowledge
summary: The difficulty of imagining what it is like not to know something you know, which leads informed people to overestimate what their audience already understands and to communicate in shorthand, abstractions and skipped steps.
selfCheck: Which terms, acronyms or steps in this message did I learn on the job rather than expect my reader to know?
If my reader had only this message and none of my background, what would they do next?
Have I asked someone outside the work to restate my point in their own words, or am I only judging clarity myself?

title: Defensiveness
summary: A self-protective reaction to perceived or anticipated threat in a conversation, in which a person spends energy guarding their image instead of taking in the message - and in which the listener's distorted hearing tends to make the speaker defensive in turn.
selfCheck: Am I about to describe what happened, or to deliver a verdict on the person who did it?
Have I signalled that the outcome is still open, or does my message sound like the decision is already made?
When I felt criticised just now, did I restate their point before I explained or justified myself?
Is the other person reacting to my content, or to a tone of superiority, certainty or hidden agenda they are picking up?

title: Describe-analyze-evaluate
summary: A three-step habit for unfamiliar or puzzling behaviour: first describe only what you observed, then list several possible explanations, and only then notice your own evaluation, so that a culture-bound judgement does not masquerade as a fact.
selfCheck: Could someone who disagrees with me still accept my description of what happened as accurate?
Have I written down more than one explanation, including one that would make this behaviour sensible where they come from?
Which of my own norms am I using to judge this, and where did I learn it?
Am I about to give feedback that starts with my verdict instead of what I observed?
steps: When a colleague's behaviour surprises or irritates you, pause before replying and write down only what you saw or heard, in words a camera could confirm.
List at least two or three different explanations for that behaviour, including at least one that would make it reasonable in the other person's context.
Name your own evaluation and its source - what you feel about the behaviour and which norm you are measuring it against.
Check the most important explanation with the person or a cultural informant using a neutral question built on your description.
Only then decide how to respond, and if you give feedback, lead with the description rather than the evaluation.

example.situation: A team lead in a global project notices that a newly transferred engineer never raises objections in design reviews and later sends concerns privately by email.
example.before: You're not engaging in reviews. If you disagree, say it in the room - sending emails afterwards looks like you're going around the team.
example.after: In the last three reviews you didn't comment during the meeting, then emailed me concerns afterwards - and they were good ones. I can think of a few reasons that might happen. How do design disagreements usually get raised on teams you've worked on?
example.why: The first version presents an evaluation ("not engaging", "going around the team") as fact; the second states the observable pattern, admits several possible explanations and asks before judging, so the engineer can explain a norm the lead may not share.

title: Difficult conversation
summary: A conversation you are tempted to avoid because the topic threatens the relationship, the other person's or your own self-image, or strong feelings on either side - raising a performance problem, disagreeing with a decision, delivering bad news or repairing a falling-out. It goes best when approached as a shared attempt to learn what happened, not a contest over who is right.

title: Direct vs. indirect feedback
summary: The contrast between stating criticism plainly, often intensified with "upgraders" such as "totally", and softening it with "downgraders", understatement or omission so the listener infers the problem; norms differ across cultures, but research shows the gap shifts with setting, status and urgency rather than following nationality alone.
selfCheck: If I strip out the softeners or intensifiers, what is the core message I am sending - and would this listener decode it the same way?
Am I about to deliver criticism in front of people who do not need to hear it?
Have I checked what the person understood, rather than assuming my politeness or bluntness landed as intended?

title: Effective Writing for Army Leaders
summary: A 1986 U.S. Department of the Army pamphlet (DA Pam 600-67) that told leaders how to enforce the Army Writing Standard - writing understood in one rapid reading - by putting the "bottom line" first, using active voice and short sentences, and coaching writers with a quick-screen edit.

title: Email
summary: The asynchronous, text-based channel most organisations use for requests, updates, decisions and records; it suits messages the reader can absorb and act on alone, and works best when each message is scannable, answer-first and explicit about what is needed and by when.

title: Ethnocentrism
summary: Treating your own culture's habits, values and ways of communicating as the normal, correct standard and judging other people's messages and behaviour against it; in workplace research it goes with lower willingness to talk across cultures and harsher judgements of out-group colleagues' competence and credibility.
selfCheck: When I called a colleague's message rude, vague or odd, was I measuring it against how people communicate where I learned to work?
Would I rate this candidate's or manager's competence the same if their accent, style and background matched mine?
Have I asked what this behaviour means in the other person's context before deciding what it means?
Who on this team have I quietly been avoiding or routing around, and is the real reason a difference in style?

title: Feedback
summary: Information given to a person about their performance or understanding, relative to a goal, so they can close the gap; on average it improves performance, but a sizeable share of feedback makes things worse, depending mainly on what it draws attention to and how much usable information it carries.

title: Feedforward
summary: A development technique popularised by executive coach Marshall Goldsmith: instead of reviewing what someone did wrong, you name one behaviour you want to improve and ask others for a couple of concrete suggestions for the future, which you listen to and thank them for without debate.
selfCheck: Have I named one behaviour I want to improve in the future, rather than asking for a verdict on the past?
When a suggestion arrived, did I say "thank you" - or did I explain why it would not work?
Am I using feedforward to avoid a conversation about a real problem that still needs to be discussed?
Which of the suggestions will I actually try, and have I told the people who gave them?
steps: Pick one specific behaviour you want to get better at, phrased as a future goal ("run tighter project kick-offs"), not a past failure.
Describe that goal briefly to a colleague who has seen you work or who knows the subject - they do not need to be your manager.
Ask for two concrete suggestions for the future, and make clear you are not asking for a review of anything that already happened.
Listen and write the suggestions down without judging, explaining or defending - the only permitted reply is "thank you".
Offer to return the favour - ask what they want to improve and give them two forward-looking suggestions in turn.
Repeat with a few different people, then choose the suggestions you will actually try and tell those colleagues what you changed.

example.situation: A project manager whose kick-off meetings regularly overrun wants to improve before the next quarter's projects start.
example.before: Can you give me some feedback on last week's kick-off? I know it ran 40 minutes over, but the client kept raising scope questions, so honestly I'm not sure what I could have done differently.
example.after: I'm working on running kick-offs that finish on time. Could you give me two ideas I could try at the next one? I'll just note them down - no need to go back over last week.
example.why: The first version invites a debate about a past meeting and opens with a defence, so the colleague has to argue to be helpful; the rewrite names a future goal, asks for a bounded number of ideas and promises not to argue, which makes it easy to offer useful suggestions.

title: First offer
summary: Deliberately naming the opening number or package in a negotiation so that it anchors the other side's expectations, and deciding - based on who knows more about the zone of possible agreement - whether to move first at all and how ambitious to be.
selfCheck: Do I know the likely range of agreement better than, as well as, or worse than the other side?
Is my opening based on my target and a reason I can say out loud, rather than on my walk-away point?
Is it ambitious enough to leave room to move but not so extreme that it could offend or end the talks?
Am I about to reveal a preference we probably share, which they could trade back to me as a concession?
If they opened first, have I re-anchored on my own numbers before replying?
steps: Before the conversation, research the market and estimate the zone of possible agreement - your walk-away point, the other side's likely walk-away point, and what comparable deals settled at.
Decide whether to move first - do so when you know the range at least as well as the other side; if they clearly know more, ask questions and let them open.
Set the offer from your ambitious target, not from your walk-away point, and make sure it is one you can justify with a real reason.
Limit the opening to the issues where your interests conflict; hold back terms you suspect both sides want anyway until you have learned their preferences.
State the number precisely and confidently, give the reason in one or two sentences, then stop talking and listen.

If they open first, do not respond to their number straight away - restate your own target, their likely limits and your alternatives to yourself, then counter from your plan rather than from their anchor.

example.situation: A marketing team lead is buying a six-month analytics retainer from a small agency she has researched; similar retainers she found ranged from $8K to $11K a month.
example.before: We don't have a fixed budget yet - what would you normally charge for something like this?
example.after: Based on the three proposals we reviewed for similar scope, we'd like to propose $8,500 a month for six months, with the weekly dashboard and quarterly review included. That reflects the market and a six-month commitment from us. How does that sit with you?
example.why: She knows the market range at least as well as the agency, so moving first lets her set the reference point near the low end with a stated rationale, instead of inviting the agency to anchor at the top of the range.

title: George Loewenstein
summary: Carnegie Mellon behavioural economist and psychologist who, with Colin Camerer and Martin Weber, put the "curse of knowledge" on the research map in 1989 and later proposed the information-gap theory of curiosity; both ideas explain why experts misjudge audiences and how to hold attention.

title: Grice's cooperative principle
summary: Philosopher Paul Grice's account of how conversation works: listeners assume a speaker is trying to contribute what the exchange needs, and expect contributions to be true (Quality), as informative as needed and no more (Quantity), relevant (Relation) and clear (Manner); departures from these expectations are read as signals of unstated meaning.
selfCheck: If my reader took every word literally and also read between the lines, what would they conclude that I did not intend?
Did I use a weaker word such as "some", "most" or "should" where a stronger one was true, and so imply the stronger one is false?
Does every sentence I am about to send answer the question that was actually asked?
Have I stated anything I believe but cannot back up, without flagging it as a belief?
Is there detail here the reader does not need to act, and detail they need that I left out?

title: High- and low-context cultures
summary: Edward T. Hall's contrast between communication in which most meaning sits in shared context, relationships and nonverbal cues (high-context) and communication in which meaning is carried mainly by explicit words (low-context); widely taught for intercultural work, but its country rankings have weak empirical support.

title: Humble inquiry
summary: Edgar Schein's practice of drawing another person out by asking questions you do not already know the answer to, out of real curiosity about them, instead of opening with your own diagnosis, advice or instructions - especially when you hold the higher status.
selfCheck: Did I ask at least one question I did not already know the answer to?
Was my question a real question, or a suggestion or a test dressed up as one?
Who talked more in that conversation, and did I learn anything that changed my view?
Did I acknowledge what they said before telling them what I think?
steps: Before the conversation, write down what you are assuming about the situation and the person, and mark which parts you have not actually checked.
Open with a question you do not know the answer to ("Walk me through how you approached this") instead of your verdict or fix.
Stop after the question and let the other person talk; resist filling the first silence with your own view.
Ask one genuine follow-up that builds on what they just said, rather than steering back to your agenda.
Acknowledge what you heard in your own words before you add any opinion, request or decision.
Only then tell - share your view or ask for what you need - and invite them to correct or add to it.

example.situation: A team lead notices a direct report delivered a client analysis in an unexpected format, a day before the client review.
example.before: This isn't the template we use. Please redo it in the standard deck format tonight so we're ready for tomorrow.
example.after: You built this differently from our usual deck - I'd like to understand why. Can you walk me through what you were going for and what you know about this client that I might not?
example.why: The first version assumes the lead already knows everything relevant and shuts the report down; the second surfaces their reasoning (perhaps the client asked for it), keeps them engaged, and still leaves time to agree a format together.

title: I-statements
summary: Raising a problem by describing the other person's specific behaviour, its concrete effect on you and how you feel about it, phrased from your own point of view ("I…") rather than as an accusation or verdict about them ("You always…").
selfCheck: Have I described a specific behaviour I could point to, or slipped in a label, a motive or an "always"?
Is my "I feel…" a real feeling, or a disguised accusation such as "I feel that you don't care"?
Have I said anything that shows I understand the other person's side of the situation?
After I speak, am I ready to listen to their reaction rather than repeat my point louder?
steps: Before speaking, name one specific, observable behaviour (what was said or done, and when) instead of a trait or a pattern word like "always" or "never".
Work out the concrete, tangible effect that behaviour has on you or your work - time lost, rework, a missed commitment.
Identify the feeling underneath, and check whether anger is masking something more precise such as worry or frustration.
Say it in the first person in roughly this order - behaviour, effect, feeling - and, if useful, a request for what you would like instead.
Add one sentence that shows you see the other person's side (their constraints, intentions or pressures) before or after your own view.
Stop and listen; expect some defensiveness, reflect back what you hear, and send a clearer second I-statement only if the first one was not understood.

example.situation: A project lead raises a recurring problem with a colleague who sends status updates late on the morning of the weekly client call.
example.before: You never get your updates in on time. You're making the whole team look unprepared in front of the client.
example.after: I know Mondays are packed for you with the support queue. When the status update reaches me after 9 a.m. on call days, I can't check the numbers before we present them, and I get anxious that we'll give the client something wrong. Could we agree on Friday afternoon as the cut-off?
example.why: The rewrite replaces a character verdict ("never", "you're making") with one observable behaviour, its concrete effect and the speaker's own feeling, acknowledges the colleague's constraint, and ends with a specific request - the combination the 2018 rating study found least likely to provoke defensiveness.

title: Illusion of transparency
summary: The tendency to overestimate how clearly other people can see our internal states - our nerves, feelings and intentions - and, by extension, how plainly our messages convey what we meant, so we under-signal and fail to check understanding.
selfCheck: Have I actually said the thing I am assuming they already picked up from my tone or face?
In this email, would a reader who could not hear my voice know whether I was joking, annoyed or serious?
Did I check what they understood, or did I take their nod as proof?
Before this presentation, am I treating my racing heart as something the audience can see?

title: Influence without authority
summary: Getting help from colleagues, other teams, bosses or clients you cannot direct by treating them as potential allies, learning what they care about and offering something they value in return - the reciprocity-based "influence model" of Allan R. Cohen and David L. Bradford.
selfCheck: Do I know what this person is measured on and worried about right now, or am I guessing?
What can I offer that they would value, and is it something I can genuinely deliver?
Have I separated what I must have from what would merely be nice?
Would I be comfortable if they saw exactly how I planned this request, or does it rely on spin?
steps: Treat the person whose help you need as a potential ally, even if past dealings were tense, and drop any story that they are simply difficult.
Write down exactly what you need from them, which parts are essential and which are nice to have, and check that the request serves the work rather than only your own ambitions.
Diagnose their world - how they are measured and rewarded, what their boss expects, what their workload and pressures are this quarter.

List the currencies they are likely to value (resources, information, help, recognition, visibility, a link to a larger purpose) and the ones you can actually offer, including cheap ones you control yourself.
Assess the relationship; if trust is low, repair it first, and adapt to how they prefer to work (data or story, email or a quick call).
Make a concrete, honest offer that trades something they value for what you need, then deliver on it and keep in touch afterwards so the relationship exists before you need it again.

example.situation: A product analyst needs an engineer on another team to add tracking events before a launch, but has no authority over the engineer's priorities.
example.before: Hi, I need these six tracking events added before Thursday's release. It's important for the launch, so please prioritise it. Thanks!
example.after: Hi - I know your team is measured on the release shipping cleanly, so I don't want to add risk. Of the six events, two are essential for the launch review (sign-up and first purchase); the rest can wait a sprint. I've written the event specs and test cases so it should be about an hour of work, and I'll credit your team in the launch metrics readout to the VP. Would Wednesday morning work, or is there a better slot?
example.why: The rewrite shows an understanding of the engineer's goals, cuts the ask to what is essential, lowers the cost by doing the preparatory work, and offers currencies the engineer may value (less effort, visibility with leadership) instead of borrowing urgency the analyst has no standing to impose.

title: Intercultural communication
summary: The study and practice of communication between people whose cultural backgrounds lead them to different interpretations and expectations about what competent communication looks like; at work it supplies the concepts, barriers and training methods used to collaborate across national, regional, occupational and other cultural lines.

title: Selling issues to leadership
aliases: getting the boss to buy in
summary: Deliberately getting senior leaders to notice, understand and act on an issue, idea or risk you see from below - by framing it in terms of goals they already own, involving allies, and choosing the timing and channel - as described in Jane E. Dutton and Susan J. Ashford's research on issue selling.
selfCheck: Can I state in one sentence which of leadership's existing goals this issue helps, and is that link honest?
Am I bringing a proposed solution and the evidence my leaders usually ask for, or only a complaint?
Who else have I involved, and would any of them be surprised to hear me raise it?
Is this the right moment and forum, or am I raising it because I am frustrated right now?
If they say no, what will I do next - and am I prepared to accept that answer?
steps: Write the issue in one sentence and link it to a goal, metric or priority your leaders already own, framed as an opportunity where honestly possible.
Find out how the decision maker likes to receive proposals - data or story, a written pre-read or a conversation - and what evidence counts in your organisation.
Build a short business case - cost, benefit, risk and what happens if nothing changes - and bring at least one concrete proposed solution, not only the problem.
Test the idea with peers and one or two respected senior people first; fold in their objections and ask who should be involved or informed.
Read the context before you raise it - is leadership listening, under pressure, or recently burned by a similar idea? - and pick a moment and channel that fit.
Raise it calmly, acknowledge any past decision you are revisiting without blaming whoever made it, and ask for one specific next step.
Follow up, report what happened, and decide deliberately whether to persist, re-bundle the issue with another priority, or let it go for now.

example.situation: A support team lead wants leadership to fund a fix for a confusing billing page that drives a large share of tickets.
example.before: Hi all, I wanted to flag (again) that the billing page is a mess. My team is drowning in tickets and nobody seems to care. Can we please prioritise this?
example.after: Proposal for Thursday's ops review: about a third of last month's support tickets trace to the billing page. A two-sprint redesign, already scoped with product, would cut handling costs and supports this year's customer-retention goal. I'd like a decision on adding it to Q1. One-page case attached; finance has checked the numbers.
example.why: The rewrite ties the issue to a goal leaders own, brings data and a solution, shows peers are already involved, and uses a scheduled forum - the packaging, involvement and process moves the research links to success - instead of venting frustration.

title: The Effects of Feedback Interventions on Performance
summary: Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi's 1996 Psychological Bulletin meta-analysis of 607 effect sizes, which found that feedback raises performance on average (d = 0.41) yet lowers it in more than a third of cases, and proposed feedback intervention theory to explain why.

title: The Illusion of Transparency and Normative Beliefs About Anxiety During Public Speaking
summary: A 2010 Current Research in Social Psychology paper in which students in a public-speaking course believed their audience saw far more nervousness than it reported, and a second survey showed that people expect high speaking anxiety to be normal.

title: Managing up
summary: The learnable skill of deliberately building a working relationship with your manager (or a senior client) that gets the best results for both of you and the organisation - by understanding their goals, pressures and preferred style, agreeing expectations, keeping them informed and being dependable - as framed by John J. Gabarro and John P. Kotter.
selfCheck: Can I name my manager's top two goals and the pressure they are under this quarter, from what they have told me rather than my guess?
Do I know whether my manager would rather read this in writing first or hear it live, and am I using that format?
Have we explicitly agreed what "done" looks like and when they want to hear from me, or am I assuming?
Is there a problem or slipping date I have not told them about yet, and why am I waiting?
Am I spending their time and goodwill on something that truly needs them, and have I brought a proposed solution?
Would I be comfortable if my manager saw exactly how I prepared for this conversation, or does it rely on flattery or spin?

title: Mehrabian's 7-38-55 rule
summary: The popular claim that only 7% of a message's meaning comes from words, 38% from tone of voice and 55% from facial expression and body language; it overgeneralises two narrow 1967 lab studies about inconsistent cues for liking, and Mehrabian himself says it does not apply to communication in general.

title: Message Equivocality, Media Selection, and Manager Performance
summary: A 1987 MIS Quarterly article by Richard Daft, Robert Lengel and Linda Klebe Trevino that turned media richness theory into a claim about managerial skill: managers tend to send ambiguous messages through rich media and clear ones through lean media, and higher performers match the two more closely.

title: Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers
summary: Opening or moving a multi-issue negotiation by putting two or three complete packages on the table at the same time, each worth about the same to you but built differently, and asking the other side which one works best for them.
selfCheck: Are my packages really equivalent in value to me, or have I hidden a preferred option among decoys?
Is every package above my walk-away point and more ambitious than my target?
Have I kept it to two or three options so the other side can compare them?
Am I ready to respond to cherry-picking with new packages instead of single concessions?
Is everything I say about the packages - including that I would accept any of them - true?
steps: List every issue that is genuinely negotiable (price, scope, timing, payment terms, support, duration) and give each a weight that reflects how much it matters to you.
For each issue, write the realistic range of options and score them so that options you prefer earn more points.

Build two or three complete packages that score about the same in total for you but trade the issues off differently - for example, higher price with faster delivery versus lower price with a longer commitment.
Check every package against your BATNA and make all of them more ambitious than your target, so there is still room to move.
Present the packages together, say you would be comfortable with any of them, and ask which one fits the other side best - or, if none does, which is closest and why.
Treat their choice as information about their priorities; if they combine the best parts of different packages, reply with a fresh set of equivalent packages rather than conceding piece by piece.

example.situation: A consulting manager is proposing terms for a follow-on analytics engagement to a client's procurement lead.
example.before: Our proposal is a 12-week engagement at $240K, paid monthly, with two analysts on site. Let us know if that works.
example.after: We've put together three options we'd be glad to do. A: 12 weeks, $240K, two analysts on site, monthly billing. B: 16 weeks, $255K, one analyst on site plus remote support, quarterly billing. C: 10 weeks, $215K, two analysts, with your team owning the dashboard build. Which of these fits your budget cycle and team best - or which is closest?
example.why: Each package is worth roughly the same to the firm, so any choice is acceptable; the client gets a real choice instead of a take-it-or-counter offer, and their pick reveals whether they care most about price, duration or internal capacity.

title: Nominal group technique
summary: A structured meeting method for generating and prioritising ideas in which people first write ideas silently and alone, then share them one at a time in a round robin, clarify them, and finally rank them privately so the group's priorities come from pooled individual votes.
selfCheck: Is my question specific enough that people could write concrete answers to it on their own?
Did I protect the silent-writing and round-robin phases from early debate or evaluation, including my own?
Did each person rank privately, so seniors' preferences were not visible before others voted?
Is this really a single-question, prioritise-and-decide meeting, or does the topic need open exploration first?
steps: Write one specific, open question on the board or shared screen and read it aloud, for example "What are the biggest obstacles to closing month-end two days faster?"
Give everyone 10-20 minutes of silent, individual writing to list as many answers as they can, with no talking.
Run a round robin - each person reads out one idea per turn, which you record verbatim and number - and keep going until the lists are exhausted; allow no debate yet.
Walk through the numbered list for clarification only, letting anyone explain an item, and merge true duplicates with the agreement of the people who raised them.
Ask each person to privately pick and rank their top five items (5 points for the most important down to 1), then tally the scores in front of the group.
Discuss the top-ranked items and the surprises in the tally, and, if the scores are close, run a second private vote before you commit to next steps.

example.situation: An operations manager runs a one-hour meeting with eight team members, including two senior leads, to decide which process problems to fix first next quarter.
example.before: Okay, open floor - what should we fix first? ... Great point, Sam [senior lead], the ticketing tool is a mess. Anyone disagree? No? Let's go with that.
example.after: Take ten minutes and write down, on your own, every process problem that slows you down. Then we'll go round the table one idea at a time, I'll number them, and everyone ranks their top five privately before we talk priorities.
example.why: The open floor lets the first senior voice anchor the room and blocks quieter people from offering ideas; silent writing and private ranking let every member contribute and weigh in equally before status and conversation shape the outcome.

title: Norbert Wiener
summary: MIT mathematician (1894-1964) who founded cybernetics, the study of control and communication in animals and machines, and carried the engineering idea of feedback - correcting action by the gap between actual result and goal - into the behavioural and social sciences.

title: Manager one-on-one meetings
summary: Recurring, scheduled conversations between a manager and one direct report, held live and focused mainly on the direct report's needs - priorities, roadblocks, feedback, wellbeing and development - rather than on the manager's status updates.

title: Open-ended questions
summary: Questions that cannot be answered with "yes", "no" or a single fact - typically starting with "what" or "how" - asked to let the other person explain in their own words, so you learn what they know, think and need rather than what you assumed.
selfCheck: Could the other person have answered my question with one word, and was that what I really wanted?
Did my next question build on their answer, or did I jump to my own agenda?
Did I ask a "why" question where a "what" or "how" would have felt less like a demand for justification?
When I needed a firm answer on a specific risk, did I ask a direct, specific question instead of a vague one?
steps: Decide what you actually need to learn - their view, the obstacles, the options - before you ask anything.
Open with "what" or "how" ("What's getting in the way?", "How did the client react?") instead of "Is", "Do" or "Did".
Stop talking and let them answer fully; resist offering a suggested answer if they pause.
Build your next question on what they just said ("You mentioned the handover - what happened there?") rather than switching topic.
Reflect back what you heard before asking another question, so the exchange does not become an interrogation.
Switch to a closed or specific question when you need a commitment, a number, or a straight answer to a known risk ("Will this slip past the 30th?").

example.situation: A team lead checks in with an engineer on a database migration that has gone quiet for a week.
example.before: Is the migration still on track for the end of the month?
example.after: What's the part of the migration you're least confident about right now?
example.why: The closed question invites a reflexive "yes"; the open one asks for an explanation and presumes there is some uncertainty, which makes it easier to surface a problem early.

title: Paraphrasing
summary: Restating, in your own words, the substance of what someone has just said - and, where it matters, the feeling and priority behind it - then checking whether you have understood them correctly before you respond with your own view.
selfCheck: Did I restate their point in my own words, or did I just repeat their phrases back like a parrot?
Did I capture what mattered to them and how they felt, not only the facts?
Did I end with a genuine check ("Have I got that right?") and accept a correction without defending myself?
Did I hold back my own view until they agreed I had understood them?
steps: Listen to the whole point without planning your reply; note the facts, what the speaker seems to feel and what seems most important to them.
Wait for a natural pause, then restate the core of their message in one or two sentences, using your own words rather than echoing theirs.
Where feelings are clearly present, name the feeling and its cause tentatively ("it sounds like the late change left you frustrated").
End with a check question such as "Have I got that right?" or "What did I miss?" and accept corrections without arguing.
If they correct you, paraphrase the corrected version; follow up with an open question if something is still unclear.
Only once they confirm you have understood, give your own perspective, answer or proposal.

example.situation: An operations lead tells a project manager that the new vendor's delivery schedule will not work for the warehouse, and the PM's instinct is to defend the schedule.
example.before: The schedule was signed off by procurement last month, so we really can't change it now. Let's just make it work.
example.after: So if I've understood you, the Tuesday deliveries land on the same morning as the weekly stock count, which means your team either delays the count or leaves trucks waiting - and you're worried we'll start paying demurrage. Is that the main problem, or is there more to it?
example.why: The rewrite restates the specific facts and the concern behind them in the PM's own words and invites correction, so the operations lead can confirm or fix the picture before anyone argues for a solution.

title: Plain language
summary: The principle of writing so that the intended readers can find what they need, understand it and use it the first time they read it, by writing for that audience in familiar words, clear structure and direct sentences.
selfCheck: Who exactly is reading this, and what do they already know about the subject?
Which terms here did I learn inside my team or field, and have I replaced or defined each one where it first appears?
Could a reader say in their own words what I want them to do next?

title: Proxemics
summary: The study of how people use and interpret physical space in communication, above all the distance they keep from one another; anthropologist Edward T. Hall described intimate, personal, social and public zones whose comfortable size varies by culture, relationship, gender and age.

title: Psychological safety
summary: A shared belief among members of a team that it is safe to take interpersonal risks - to ask a question, admit a mistake, raise a concern or disagree - without being embarrassed, rejected or punished for it.

title: Rapport
summary: A shared, momentary quality of an interaction in which both people are attentive to each other, feel mutual warmth and move in coordination; it belongs to the pair rather than to either person, and it makes disclosure and cooperation easier.
selfCheck: Did I give this person my full attention, or was part of me on my screen or my next point?
Did I learn one thing about them as a person before we got into the business?
Before a hard negotiation or tense thread, have we ever spoken live, even for five minutes?
Did the setting and their cues invite small talk, or did they signal they wanted to get straight to work?
Am I trying to connect, or performing techniques such as copying their posture?

title: Ray Tomlinson
summary: BBN engineer (1941-2016) who in 1971 sent the first messages between users on different ARPANET computers, chose the "@" that still separates user from host in every address, and co-wrote the 1973 header standard that made From, Subject and Date part of every message.

title: Risk numbers as natural frequencies
summary: Restating percentages and conditional probabilities as whole-number counts drawn from one stated group ("of 10,000 orders, 20 are fraudulent and 18 of those get flagged"), so listeners can see base rates, hits and false alarms and work out what a result actually means.
selfCheck: Have I stated the reference group ("out of every 1,000 ...") before giving any count?
Can my listener see how many cases are false alarms, not just how many real cases are caught?
Am I comparing options with the same denominator and in absolute terms rather than "doubled" or "halved"?
Does every number in my sentence clearly belong to one named group?
If someone asked "so of the ones flagged, how many are real?", have I already answered it?
steps: Pick one reference group large enough that every count comes out as a whole number (1,000 or 10,000 is usual) and name it in the first sentence.
Split that group by the base rate first - how many have the condition, defect or event and how many do not.
Apply the detection or hit rate inside the first subgroup and the false-alarm rate inside the second, and write each result as a count.
Answer the decision question as "X out of Y" - for example, how many of all flagged cases are real - instead of quoting the test's accuracy.
Keep the same denominator for every option you compare, and give absolute changes ("from 20 to 10 in 1,000") rather than relative ones ("halved").
Tie every number to its group in the wording ("of the 9,980 legitimate orders, about 500 are flagged") and, for a live audience, sketch the counts as a simple frequency tree.

example.situation: A risk analyst briefs the head of operations on whether to auto-cancel every order a new fraud model flags.
example.before: The model catches 90% of fraud with only a 5% false-positive rate, so a flagged order is very likely fraudulent - I'd auto-cancel them.
example.after: Out of every 10,000 orders, about 20 are fraudulent and the model flags 18 of them. Of the other 9,980 legitimate orders it also flags about 500. So of roughly 518 flagged orders, only 18 - about 1 in 30 - are fraud. Auto-cancelling would block about 500 good customers to stop 18 bad ones; I suggest manual review instead.
example.why: The before version quotes the model's accuracy and invites the listener to ignore how rare fraud is; the counts make the base rate and the false alarms visible, so the leader can see that most flags are wrong and decide on that basis.

title: Self-distancing strategies
summary: Stepping back from your own point of view before or after a nerve-racking moment - by talking to yourself by name or as "you", or by picturing the scene as an outside observer would - so that you judge the stakes and your own salience more like the audience does.
selfCheck: If I described this moment to myself by name, what would I tell me to do next?
From a colleague's seat, how much of this meeting is actually about me?
Am I replaying this slip in the first person, and what would an observer say mattered instead?
Have I turned the distanced view into one concrete next action?
steps: Before the meeting or talk, write or say two or three sentences of self-talk using your own name or "you" instead of "I" (for example, "Sam, you know this material; your job is to explain it").
Picture the room from the back row or from a colleague's seat, not through your own eyes, and ask what that observer would actually notice.
Notice what the observer is busy with - their own agenda, notes and next point - and adjust your estimate of how much attention you will get.
Turn the distanced view into one concrete action, such as the opening line, the one question you will ask or the one-sentence correction you will use if you slip.
Afterwards, review the moment the same way ("What did Sam do well? What would Sam change?") instead of replaying it in the first person.

example.situation: An analyst is about to raise a concern about a vendor's numbers in a cross-team review where she is the most junior person.
example.before: I'm going to sound naive. Everyone will remember that I'm the one who didn't get the model. I'll just keep quiet and email the lead later.
example.after: Priya, picture this from the back of the room: eight people focused on their own slides. You spotted a real gap. Ask one short question about the churn assumption, then let the lead answer.
example.why: Naming herself and taking an observer's view shrinks the imagined spotlight and turns vague dread into one specific, low-cost contribution, which is the pattern lab studies link to less distress and better performance.

title: Situation-Behavior-Impact
summary: A three-part way to give feedback developed at the Center for Creative Leadership: name the specific situation, describe the observable behaviour, and say what impact it had on you - optionally followed by asking about the person's intent.
selfCheck: Could the other person picture the exact moment I mean, or did I say something vague like "lately"?
Is my behaviour description something a camera could record, or did I slip in a judgement or guess at a motive?
Have I said what the impact actually was, rather than assuming they already know?
Did I leave room to ask about their intent and listen before deciding what should change?
steps: Pin down the situation - the specific meeting, document or moment, with a time and place ("in Tuesday's 10 a.m. client call"), not "lately" or "last week".
Describe the behaviour as something a camera could have recorded - words said, actions taken - and strip out labels such as "rude", "lazy" or "great attitude".
State the impact the behaviour had on you, the team or the work, in your own voice, naming a concrete consequence and, if useful, your reaction (frustrated, relieved, proud).
For redirecting feedback, stop and ask about intent ("What were you aiming for there?") and listen before proposing any fix.
Agree together on what to keep doing or what to try next time, and give the feedback close to the event while it is still fresh.
Use the same three parts for positive feedback, so the person knows exactly which behaviour to repeat.

example.situation: A team lead gives feedback to an analyst who presented the quarterly numbers at a leadership review.
example.before: You came across as really unprepared today and kind of defensive. You need to step up your game before the next one.
example.after: In this morning's quarterly review with the VPs, when Priya asked where the churn figure came from, you said 'I'd have to check' and moved on. The VPs then questioned two other numbers and we lost ten minutes of the agenda, and I was worried they'd discount the whole forecast. What was going on for you at that point?
example.why: The rewrite swaps verdicts ("unprepared", "defensive") for a time-stamped situation, an observable behaviour and a concrete impact, then asks about intent - so the analyst can see exactly what to change and has room to explain instead of defending their character.

title: Public speaking anxiety
summary: Fear and physical arousal triggered by having to speak in front of others - from a team update to a conference talk - that pushes people to avoid speaking, over-script, or deliver less well than they could.
selfCheck: Am I declining this presentation because it is not my job, or because I am afraid of it?
Have I rehearsed this out loud, standing, at least once - or only read my notes silently?
Am I assuming the audience can see my nerves as clearly as I can feel them?
What is the one point I need them to leave with, if everything else goes badly?
Afterwards, am I judging the talk by how I felt or by what the audience actually did with it?

title: Spotlight effect
aliases: overestimating how much others notice us
summary: The tendency to overestimate how much other people notice, remember and judge our appearance, words and slip-ups, which makes communicators hold back, over-apologise and dwell on small mistakes that the audience barely registered.
selfCheck: Am I staying quiet because I think everyone will remember this one comment, when they are mostly thinking about their own contributions?
If a colleague had made the slip I just made, would I still be thinking about it tomorrow?
Am I about to spend the first minute of my talk apologising for something the audience has not noticed?
If I picture this meeting from the back of the room instead of through my own eyes, how big does my moment really look?

title: Stakeholder mapping
summary: A planning technique for listing everyone who can affect or is affected by a decision or change, sorting them by how much power and interest they have, and using that picture to decide whom to involve, consult or inform, and with what message.
selfCheck: Who could stop or slow this, and have I spoken to them directly rather than assuming their view?
Who will be most affected but has the least say, and how will they hear about it before it lands?
Does each group's message answer their concern, or is it the same message I would send everyone?
When did I last update this map, and has anyone's stance or influence changed since?
steps: Write down the decision or change in one sentence and set the boundary - which teams, customers, regulators and time frame are in scope.
List everyone who can affect it or will be affected by it, then ask two or three colleagues outside your team who is missing, including people with little voice.

For each stakeholder, note their main interest or concern, whether they currently support, oppose or are undecided, and what power they hold (budget, sign-off, expertise, reputation, ability to block).
Place each one on a power-versus-interest grid and pick an engagement level - partner closely, keep satisfied, consult, or keep informed.
For each group, decide who will talk to them, the one message that speaks to their interest, the channel and how often - then put that in a communication plan.
Test the map by talking to the stakeholders themselves, and revisit it at each milestone, because power, interest and stance shift.

example.situation: An operations manager is replacing the team's expense-claims tool and has a go-live date in six weeks.
example.before: Plan: send one all-staff email two weeks before go-live announcing the new tool, with a link to the user guide.
example.after: Map: Finance director (high power, high interest, undecided) - weekly check-in, co-own the cut-over date. Payroll lead (high power, low interest) - one briefing on the export file, sign-off by week 3. Frequent travellers in sales (low power, high interest, worried about slower refunds) - invite two to test in week 2, answer the refund-time question in every message. Everyone else - short email at go-live and a two-minute video.
example.why: The single email treated everyone as one audience; the map shows who can block the launch, who will feel it most and what each needs to hear, so the manager spends attention where a surprise would be costly.

title: Teach-back
summary: Checking whether an explanation landed by asking the other person to explain it back, or show it, in their own words - framed as a test of how clearly you explained rather than of what they know - and re-explaining until their version is right.
selfCheck: Did I ask them to say it in their own words, or did I accept a nod or a "makes sense"?
Did I frame the check as testing my explanation, not their competence?
Which one or two points would cause real damage if misunderstood, and did I check those?
When their restatement was off, did I re-explain differently rather than repeat myself louder?
steps: Pick the one to three points the other person must get right to act - a deadline, a decision, a sequence of steps - rather than checking everything.
Explain each point in plain, specific language, one point at a time.
Take ownership of the check out loud, for example "I want to make sure I explained that clearly."
Ask an open request to restate or demonstrate ("How will you walk the client through this?"), never a yes/no question such as "Does that make sense?"
Listen for gaps or errors; if you hear one, re-explain that part differently and ask again until their version is accurate.
Close by confirming the agreed version in writing where it matters (a recap message or ticket).

example.situation: A team lead hands over an urgent client escalation to a colleague before going on leave.
example.before: So that's the background - escalate to Priya's team if the patch fails, and keep the client posted. Does that all make sense?
example.after: I've thrown a lot at you, so let me check I explained it well. If the patch fails on Thursday, what are your next two moves, and who hears from you first?
example.why: The yes/no check invites a polite "yes"; the open request surfaces the missing piece (who to call first) while the lead can still fix it, and frames any gap as the explainer's problem.

title: The Culture Map
aliases: Breaking Through the Invisible Boundaries of Global Business
summary: Erin Meyer's 2014 business book and framework that compares national cultures on eight workplace scales - communicating, evaluating, persuading, leading, deciding, trusting, disagreeing and scheduling - and asks managers to read differences relative to their own position rather than in absolute terms.

title: Thomas Gilovich
summary: Cornell social psychologist who, with Kenneth Savitsky and Victoria Medvec, named and tested the illusion of transparency (1998) and the spotlight effect (2000), the two egocentric biases that make speakers think their nerves, slips and intentions are far more visible than they are.

title: The Relative Effectiveness of Active Listening in Initial Interactions
summary: A 2014 International Journal of Listening experiment in which 115 students talked with trained partners who either paraphrased and asked follow-up questions, gave advice, or simply acknowledged; active listening made speakers feel more understood, but it was not liked more than advice.

title: William Strunk Jr.
summary: Cornell English professor (1869-1946) whose 1918 classroom handbook, The Elements of Style, set out short imperative rules such as using the active voice and omitting needless words; revised by his former student E. B. White in 1959, it became the best-known American writing guide.

title: Words of estimative probability
summary: Stating how likely something is with an agreed set of likelihood words, each tied to a numeric range that is shown next to the word, so that "likely" means the same thing to the writer and every reader.
selfCheck: If three readers each wrote down the percentage they think my likelihood word means, would their numbers land in the same range as mine?
Have I put the number next to the word, or am I relying on readers to look up a key they will probably skip?
Am I using "could", "may" or "possible" to hedge when I actually have an estimate I am reluctant to commit to?
Have I kept my confidence in the evidence separate from the likelihood of the event?
steps: Agree a short likelihood scale with your team or client before you need it - for example remote (under 5%), unlikely (20-45%), roughly even (45-55%), likely (55-80%), very likely (80-95%) - with ranges that do not overlap.
Before writing a forecast, decide your own number or range first, then pick the one word on the scale whose range contains it.
Put the numeric range in brackets right after the word in the text itself ("likely (55-80%)"), not in a footnote, appendix or hover text.
Keep likelihood (how probable the event is) separate from confidence (how solid your evidence is), and say each in its own sentence.
Reserve "possible", "could" and "may" for cases where you genuinely cannot estimate the odds, and say so rather than using them as softeners.
Use the same words with the same meanings in every report, and add a short key whenever a new reader joins the distribution.

example.situation: A consultant updates a client steering committee on whether a system migration will hit its go-live date.
example.before: There is a real possibility we could miss the March 1 go-live, although the team is working hard and it may well still be achievable.
example.after: We judge it unlikely (20-45%) that we hit the March 1 go-live; very likely (80-95%) by March 22. We have moderate confidence: the estimate rests on two weeks of test-defect data. Decision needed by Friday: hold the date with reduced scope, or move it.
example.why: The before version could be read anywhere from a small risk to a probable slip; the after version gives one shared range, separates odds from confidence, and turns the forecast into a decision the committee can make.

title: Zoom fatigue
summary: The tiredness and depletion people report after video meetings, linked to sustained close-up eye contact, the extra effort of sending and reading nonverbal cues on screen, watching a self-view and being kept still in front of a camera; it drains the energy people bring to later meetings and makes them less likely to speak up.
selfCheck: Does this conversation need video at all, or would a phone call, a shared document or a written update do the job?
Have I booked video meetings back to back with no break to stand up, move or look away from the screen?
Am I watching my own tile more than the people I am talking to, and could I hide self-view?
Did I make it clear that cameras are optional for this meeting, especially for newer team members?
Did people have a moment to connect as a group, or did we go straight into a wall of faces and slides?
